title: Does Organic Farming Grow Less Food?

generation.notes: Rebuilt package adds Ponisio L95-L99 (recorded on organic-farming-needs-more-land-produce): s07 now carries the authors' warning that reporting bias may make even their estimate an overestimate. Ponisio's study counts and Clark and Tilman's Europe/North America scope could not be recorded, so neither is stated; s21 carries Clark and Tilman's limit only as the cited local-scale caveat.

sentences.text: Picture two fields growing the same crop, one farmed organically and one not. At harvest, does the organic field come up short, and by how much?
Ask around and you hear both answers with total confidence: organic grows less, or organic grows just as much.

assertions.text: Several sources say organic farming yields less than conventional farming.
Other sources say organic farming yields as much as conventional farming or more.

sentences.text: And the answer sets up a second question: if organic does grow less, is it still the greener choice?

sections.name: question-1
sections.title: Does organic farming really grow less food?

sentences.text: AsapSCIENCE told its viewers that "organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones".

assertions.text: AsapSCIENCE says organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones.

quote.text: organic crop yields are 25% lower on average than conventional ones
quote.speaker: AsapSCIENCE

sentences.text: Mark Hyman says the opposite: "you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals".

assertions.text: Mark Hyman says you can grow as much food or more without the chemicals conventional farming uses.

quote.text: you can grow as much food or more food better food without all those chemicals
quote.speaker: Mark Hyman

sentences.text: So who is right?

A meta-analysis by Lauren Ponisio and colleagues pooled side-by-side yield comparisons and found organic yields 19.2% lower than conventional, with a likely range of 15.5 to 22.9%, and the authors warn that even this may overstate the gap, because the published studies lean towards reporting bigger conventional wins.
sentences.note: 'Likely range' is the 95% credible interval L65 gives. The warning is the authors' own (L95: a bias towards reporting higher conventional to organic yield ratios, so the estimate may still be an overestimate; L99: 'potentially overestimated').

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues' meta-analysis found organic yields 19.2% lower than conventional yields, with a 95% credible interval from 15.5% to 22.9%.
qualifications: The same sentence carries the authors' warning that the estimate may overstate the gap (s07.b); s11 and s12 carry the dissenting clinical report in the same section.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues found a bias in the literature towards reporting higher conventional to organic yield ratios, so their 15.5% to 22.9% yield gap may still be an overestimate.

sentences.text: Conventional came out ahead for every crop type the study grouped, and for most of those types the gap was about the same size.

assertions.text: In Ponisio's meta-analysis conventional yields were significantly higher than organic for all crop types, and the yield ratios of most crop types did not differ significantly from one another.

sentences.text: That gap is real, but it is smaller than the ones earlier meta-analyses had reported.

assertions.text: Ponisio's meta-analysis found a smaller organic yield gap than recent earlier meta-analyses had reported.

sentences.text: Why lower at all? A review of organic food and health, citing earlier work, points to fertiliser: in organic systems crop yield is typically limited by how much nitrogen the plants can get, which is not the case in conventional systems.

assertions.text: Mie and colleagues' review, citing earlier work, says crop yield is typically limited by plant nitrogen availability in organic but not in conventional systems.
qualifications: The sentence says the review cites earlier work rather than analysing yields itself.

sentences.text: Not everyone agrees: a clinical report for pediatricians says well-designed farming studies show organic yields comparable to conventional farming.

assertions.text: The AAP clinical report says well-designed farming studies demonstrate organic yields comparable to those of conventional farming techniques.

sentences.text: But in the report's summary, the part we could read, that is one sentence, with no yield figure and no studies named.
sentences.note: The corpus holds the AAP abstract only; the passage is the whole of what it says on yields.

assertions.text: The AAP report's abstract states comparable yields in one sentence without giving a yield figure or naming the studies.

sentences.text: So on the pooled data, yes: organic fields grew less, by roughly a fifth or perhaps a little less, but where crops were rotated or grown in mixtures the gap shrank to about 8 or 9%.

assertions.text: On Ponisio's pooled comparisons organic yields were lower than conventional, by 19.2% on average.
qualifications: 'or perhaps a little less' points back to the authors' overstatement warning in s07 (s13.b); the clause on rotations and mixtures gives the narrower gap under diversification (s13.c); s11 and s12 present the dissenting clinical report just before this answer.

assertions.text: Ponisio and colleagues say their yield-gap estimate may still be an overestimate.
Ponisio and colleagues found the yield gap dropped to 9% with multi-cropping and 8% with crop rotations.

sentences.note: 'Grown in mixtures' glosses multi-cropping (9 +/- 4%), 'rotated' crop rotations (8 +/- 5%), both at L99; 'about' carries the +/- ranges.

sentences.text: Which raises the next question: if each organic field grows less, does organic need more land for the same food, and does that undo its green reputation?

sections.name: question-2
sections.title: Is organic farming actually better for the planet?

sentences.text: Harvard Health put it plainly: "Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet".

assertions.text: Harvard Health says organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet.

quote.text: Organic foods are clearly healthier for the planet
quote.speaker: Harvard Health

sentences.text: The same pediatric report agrees, saying organic farming "has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches".

assertions.text: The AAP clinical report says organic farming has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches.

quote.text: has been demonstrated to have less environmental impact than conventional approaches

qualifications: s17 to s22 give the per-unit-of-food comparison that qualifies it.

sentences.text: But a meta-analysis by Clark and Tilman measured the impacts per unit of food, not per field, using studies that assessed both systems within the same publication.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman compared organic and conventional systems per unit of food, limiting comparisons to within the same publication.

sentences.note: The reviewer asked for Clark and Tilman's Europe/North America high-input scope. It is at L468-L476, outside the only cited range for this document (L461-L467 ends at 'for all indicators examined'), and an evidence agent established it cannot be recorded: the store keeps one verdict per claim and document, and this document is already cited for that claim. So the scope is not stated; the sentence keeps its existing caveat (per unit of food, within-publication comparisons) and s21 carries the authors' cited local-scale limit.

sentences.text: Measured that way, organic systems needed 25 to 110% more land.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems required 25% to 110% more land than conventional systems.

sentences.text: They used 15% less energy, but had 37% higher eutrophication potential, a measure of nutrient pollution.
sentences.note: 'Nutrient pollution' glosses eutrophication potential; the document defines it at L202 (outside the cited lines).

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems used 15% less energy and had 37% higher eutrophication potential than conventional systems.

sentences.text: Greenhouse gas emissions came out similar, because relying on manure turns more of a farm's nitrogen into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic and conventional systems did not significantly differ in greenhouse gas emissions.
Reliance on manure increases the share of reactive nitrogen in organic systems that turns into nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas, causing similar emissions.

sentences.text: The authors add that these are comparisons at a local scale, and the picture might differ regionally, nationally or globally.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman say their within-publication results indicate differences at a local scale and that impacts might differ at a regional, national or global scale.

sentences.text: And they warn against reading this as a win for conventional farming, which uses more energy and relies on high fertiliser, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm health and the environment.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman say organic systems' higher land use and eutrophication should not be taken to mean conventional systems are more sustainable, since conventional practices need more energy and rely on high nutrient, herbicide and pesticide inputs that can harm human health and the environment.

sentences.text: What does dwarf the organic question is the food itself: on every indicator they examined, ruminant meats had 20 to 100 times the impacts of plant-based foods, a difference far larger than the one between farming systems.

assertions.text: Clark and Tilman found ruminant meats have impacts 20 to 100 times those of plant-based foods for all indicators examined, and that the difference between foods is large compared to the difference between production systems.

sentences.text: So per unit of food, organic is not clearly greener: it trades lower energy use for more land and more nutrient pollution, with emissions about even.

assertions.text: Per unit of food, organic systems used less energy, needed more land, had higher eutrophication potential and similar greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional systems.
qualifications: s22 carries the authors' warning that this does not make conventional more sustainable; s21 the local-scale limit.

sentences.text: The next time a label or a video says organic grows just as much, ask which studies, and how many.
And when something is sold as better for the planet, ask: better per what? Per plate of food, the answer here was mixed.
